claim: The reference genome IPO323 contains 4753 TE copies grouped into 30 families with highly variable copy numbers.
source: We detected 4753 TE copies, grouped into 30 families with highly variable copy numbers in the reference genome IPO323 (Figure 2—source data 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the reference genome analysis and cited figures.

claim: A total of 18,864 TE insertions grouping into 2465 individual loci were detected across 284 genomes.
source: We found robust evidence for a total of 18,864 TE insertions grouping into 2465 individual loci.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational detection of TE insertions across the analyzed genomes.

claim: 35.5% of TE loci (n = 876) are singleton TEs present in only one isolate.
source: Of these loci, 35.5% (n = 876) have singleton TEs (i.e., this locus is only present in one isolate: Figure 2A, Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by frequency analysis of TE insertions across isolates.

claim: 95.1% of TE loci (2345 loci) have a TE frequency below 1%.
source: An overwhelming proportion of loci (2345 loci or 95.1%) have a TE frequency below 1%.
evidence: The claim is supported by frequency distribution analysis of TE loci.

claim: PacBio long-read data confirmed the exact location of 71% (22 of 31) of singleton insertions among seven isolates.
source: Aligned PacBio reads confirmed the exact location of 71% (22 of 31 singleton insertions among seven isolates; see Materials and methods for further details).
evidence: The claim is supported by validation using PacBio long-read sequencing data.

claim: The density of TE loci on accessory chromosomes is almost twice the density found on core chromosomes (102 vs 58 TEs per Mb).
source: The density of TE loci on accessory chromosomes, which are not shared among all isolates of the species, is almost twice the density found on core chromosomes (102 vs 58 TEs per Mb; Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by density calculations and referenced figures showing TE distribution.

claim: Higher TE density on accessory chromosomes suggests relaxed selection against TE insertion on functionally dispensable and gene-poor accessory chromosomes.
source: This suggests relaxed selection against TE insertion on the functionally dispensable and gene-poor accessory chromosomes.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed density differences between chromosome types.

claim: 88.2% of all TE copies belong to class I/retrotransposons (n = 2175).
source: TEs grouped into 23 families and 11 superfamilies, with 88.2% of all copies belonging to class I/retrotransposons (n = 2175; Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by classification data of TE copies.

claim: RLG/Gypsy (n = 1483) and RLC/Copia (n = 623) elements constitute the largest long terminal repeats (LTR) superfamilies.
source: RLG/Gypsy (n = 1483) and RLC/Copia (n = 623) elements constitute the largest long terminal repeats (LTR) superfamilies.
evidence: The claim is supported by counts of TE superfamilies.

claim: Class II/DNA transposons are dominated by DHH/Helitron (n = 249).
source: Class II/DNA transposons are dominated by DHH/Helitron (n = 249).
evidence: The claim is supported by counts of DNA transposon families.

claim: 153 loci with TEs inserted into genes were detected, with most insertions being singletons (44.7%; n = 68) or of very low frequency.
source: We detected 153 loci with TEs inserted into genes with most of the insertions being singletons (44.7%; n = 68) or of very low frequency (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TE insertions within genes.

claim: TE insertions into exonic sequences were less frequent than expected compared to insertions into up- and downstream regions, consistent with effective purifying selection.
source: Overall, TE insertions into exonic sequences were less frequent than expected compared to insertions into up- and downstream regions, which is consistent with effective purifying selection (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by observed distribution patterns and interpreted as evidence of selection.

claim: Insertions into introns were strongly under-represented, likely due to the small size of most fungal introns (~50–100 bp) and the high probability of disrupting splicing or adjacent coding sequences.
source: Insertions into introns were also strongly under-represented, likely due to the small size of most fungal introns (~50–100 bp) and the high probability of disrupting splicing or adjacent coding sequences.
evidence: The claim is supported by observed patterns and explained through inference about intron size and function.

claim: TE insertions 800–1000 bp away from coding sequences of a focal gene were under-represented.
source: We also found that insertions 800–1000 bp away from coding sequences of a focal gene were under-represented.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TE insertion distances from genes.

claim: The average spacing between genes is 1.744 kb.
source: Given the high gene density, with an average spacing between genes of 1.744 kb, TE insertions within 800–1000 bp of a coding gene tend to be near adjacent genes already.
evidence: The claim is supported by genome annotation data.

claim: Seven candidate loci possibly underlying local adaptation were identified (six in North America, one in Europe).
source: Based on these criteria, we obtained seven candidate loci possibly underlying local adaptation (six in North America, one in Europe; Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by selection scan analysis and frequency criteria.

claim: All seven candidate adaptive loci carry inserted retrotransposons with four RLG_Luna, one RLG_Mercurius, and one RLG_Deimos.
source: All loci carry inserted retrotransposons with four RLG_Luna, one RLG_Mercurius, and one RLG_Deimos.
evidence: The claim is supported by classification of TEs at candidate loci.

claim: One TE insertion is 3815 bp downstream of a gene encoding an RTA1-like protein and 5785 bp upstream of a gene encoding a protein kinase domain.
source: One TE insertion is 3815 bp downstream of a gene encoding an RTA1-like protein, which can function as transporters with a transmembrane domain and have been associated with resistance against several antifungal compounds (Soustre et al., 1996). The insertion is also 5785 bp upstream of a gene encoding a protein kinase domain (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic location data and cited literature on RTA1 function.

claim: The TE insertion near the RTA1-like protein gene was not detected in the Middle East or the two European populations and was at low frequencies in the Australian (3.7%) and North American 1990 (1.7%) populations, but increased to 53% in the North American 2015 population (FST = 0.42).
source: The TE insertion was not detected in the Middle East or the two European populations and was at low frequencies in the Australian (3.7%) and North American 1990 (1.7%) populations, but increased to 53% of all isolates in the North American 2015 population (fixation index FST = 0.42; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by frequency data across populations.

claim: Isolates that carry the TE insertion near the RTA1-like protein gene show significantly higher resistance to azole antifungal compounds.
source: Isolates that carry the insertion show a significantly higher resistance to azole antifungal compounds (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental fungicide resistance assays.

claim: The TE insertion at two loci was positively associated with higher levels of fungicide resistance.
source: We found that the insertion of TEs at two loci was positively associated with higher levels of fungicide resistance, suggesting that the adaptation was mediated by the TE (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental testing of fungicide resistance.

claim: TE frequencies across loci showed only weak clustering by geographic origin with the Australian population being the most distinct.
source: In stark contrast, TE frequencies across loci showed only weak clustering by geographic origin with the Australian population being the most distinct (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by principal component analysis of TE frequencies.

claim: There was surprisingly strong differentiation of the two North American populations sampled at a 25-year interval in the same field in Oregon.
source: We found a surprisingly strong differentiation of the two North American populations sampled at a 25-year interval in the same field in Oregon.
evidence: The claim is supported by principal component analysis showing population differentiation.

claim: The Middle Eastern population from Israel showed generally lower TE numbers.
source: We found generally lower TE numbers in the Middle Eastern population from Israel (Figure 6A–C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), which is close to the pathogen's center of origin (Stukenbrock et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by TE count data and cited literature on the center of origin.

claim: Populations that underwent at least one migration bottleneck showed a substantial burst of TEs across all major superfamilies.
source: Populations that underwent at least one migration bottleneck showed a substantial burst of TEs across all major superfamilies.
evidence: The claim is supported by TE count comparisons across populations with known demographic histories.

claim: A second stark increase in TE content occurred in the North American population sampled in 2015 at the same site as the population from 1990.
source: We found a second stark increase in TE content in the North American population sampled in 2015 at the same site as the population from 1990.
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal comparison of TE counts at the same location.

claim: The isolate with the lowest number of analyzed TEs collected in 2015 was comparable to the isolate with the highest number of TEs at the same site in 1990.
source: Strikingly, the isolate with the lowest number of analyzed TEs collected in 2015 was comparable to the isolate with the highest number of TEs at the same site in 1990.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of TE count ranges between temporal populations.

claim: The first step of expansions observed in Europe compared to the Middle East (Israel) was associated with an upwards shift in allele frequencies, consistent with transposition activity creating new copies and stronger purifying selection in the Middle East.
source: We found that the first step of expansions observed in Europe compared to the Middle East (Israel) was associated with an upwards shift in allele frequencies. This is consistent with transposition activity creating new copies in the genomes and stronger purifying selection in the Middle East.
evidence: The claim is supported by frequency spectrum analysis and interpreted through population genetic theory.

claim: The North American populations showed signatures consistent with relaxation of selection against TEs (i.e., fewer low-frequency TEs).
source: Similarly, the North American populations showed also signatures consistent with relaxation of selection against TEs (i.e., fewer low-frequency TEs).
evidence: The claim is supported by frequency spectrum analysis interpreted as evidence of relaxed selection.

claim: There was a significant difference (two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, two-sided) in the curve shapes between the population from the Middle East and North America 2015.
source: We found a significant difference (two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, two-sided) in the curve shapes between the population from the Middle East and North America 2015 (Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical testing of frequency distributions.

claim: The expansions were mostly driven by RLG elements including the families Luna, Sol, and Venus, the RLC family Deimos, and the LINE family Lucy.
source: We analyzed variation in TE copy numbers across families and found that the expansions were mostly driven by RLG elements including the families Luna, Sol, and Venus, the RLC family Deimos, and the LINE family Lucy (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by family-specific TE copy number analysis.

claim: A North American–specific burst in DHH elements of the family Ada occurred (increase from 4.6 to 6.1 copies on average per isolate).
source: We also found a North American–specific burst in DHH elements of the family Ada (increase from 4.6 to 6.1 copies on average per isolate), an increase specific to Swiss populations in LINE elements, and an increase in RLC elements in the Australian and the two North American populations.
evidence: The claim is supported by population-specific TE copy number analysis.

claim: Reference-quality genomes confirmed that the increase in TEs was driven by LINE, RLG, and RLC families in Australia and DHH, RLG, and RLC families in North America.
source: The reference-quality genomes confirmed also that the increase in TEs was driven by LINE, RLG, and RLC families in Australia and DHH, RLG, and RLC families in North America (Badet et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by independent analysis of reference-quality genomes and cited literature.

claim: There was a strong increase in the total TE length in populations outside the Middle East center of origin and a second increase between the two North American populations.
source: We estimated the cumulative length of TE insertions based on the length of the corresponding TE consensus sequences and found a strong increase in the total TE length in populations outside the Middle East center of origin and a second increase between the two North American populations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by cumulative TE length calculations.

claim: Genome assemblies across different populations carry generally >99% complete BUSCO gene sets, matching the completeness of reference-quality genomes of the same species.
source: Genome assemblies across different populations carry generally >99% complete BUSCO gene sets, matching the completeness of reference-quality genomes of the same species (Badet et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by BUSCO completeness analysis and comparison to reference genomes.

claim: GC content was inversely correlated with genome size consistent with the expansion of repetitive regions having generally low GC content.
source: GC content was inversely correlated with genome size consistent with the expansion of repetitive regions having generally low GC content (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis and interpreted through knowledge of repetitive sequence composition.

claim: The Middle East, Australia, as well as the two older European and North American populations had the smallest core genome sizes.
source: We found that the core genome size varied substantially among populations with the Middle East, Australia, as well as the two older European and North American populations having the smallest core genome sizes (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by genome size measurements across populations.

claim: There was a notable increase in core genome size in both the more recent European and North American populations.
source: We found a notable increase in core genome size in both the more recent European and North American populations.
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal comparison of genome sizes.

claim: The increase in core genome size is positively correlated with the count and cumulative length of all inserted TEs.
source: The increase in core genome size is positively correlated with the count and cumulative length of all inserted TEs (Figure 7D, E and G) and negatively correlated with the genome-wide GC content (Figure 7F,G, Benjamini and Speed, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis between genome size and TE metrics.

claim: The cumulative length of inserted TEs represents between 4.8% and 184% of the variable genome segment defined for the species or 0.2–2.6% of the estimated genome size per isolate.
source: We found that the cumulative length of inserted TEs represents between 4.8% and 184% of the variable genome segment defined for the species or 0.2–2.6% of the estimated genome size per isolate (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by calculations of TE contribution to genome size variation.

claim: TEs are major drivers of genome instability and epigenetic change.
source: Transposable elements (TEs) are mobile repetitive DNA sequences with the ability to independently insert into new regions of the genome. TEs are major drivers of genome instability and epigenetic change (Eichler and Sankoff, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on TE effects.

claim: Insertion of TEs can disrupt coding sequences, trigger chromosomal rearrangements, or alter expression profiles of adjacent genes.
source: Insertion of TEs can disrupt coding sequences, trigger chromosomal rearrangements, or alter expression profiles of adjacent genes (Lim, 1988; Petrov et al., 2003; Slotkin and Martienssen, 2007; Hollister and Gaut, 2009; Oliver et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple cited studies on TE insertion effects.

claim: Most TE insertions have neutral or deleterious effects upon insertions.
source: However, most TE insertions have neutral or deleterious effects upon insertions.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge in population genetics.

claim: Purifying selection is expected to rapidly eliminate deleterious insertions from populations unless constrained by genetic drift.
source: Purifying selection is expected to rapidly eliminate deleterious insertions from populations unless constrained by genetic drift (Walser et al., 2006; Baucom et al., 2009; Cridland et al., 2013; Stuart et al., 2016; Lai et al., 2017; Stritt et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on selection against deleterious TEs.

claim: Across eukaryotes, epigenetic silencing is a shared defense mechanism against TEs.
source: Across eukaryotes, epigenetic silencing is a shared defense mechanism against TEs (Slotkin and Martienssen, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on TE defense mechanisms.

claim: Fungi evolved an additional and highly specific defense system introducing repeat-induced point (RIP) mutations into any nearly identical set of sequences.
source: Fungi evolved an additional and highly specific defense system introducing repeat-induced point (RIP) mutations into any nearly identical set of sequences.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of fungal genome defense mechanisms.

claim: TEs tend to expand through family-specific bursts of transposition followed by prolonged phases of transposition inactivity.
source: TEs tend to expand through family-specific bursts of transposition followed by prolonged phases of transposition inactivity.
evidence: The claim is based on established patterns of TE activity.

claim: Bursts of insertions of different retrotransposon families were observed across eukaryotic lineages including Homo sapiens, Zea mays, Oryza sativa, and Blumeria graminis.
source: Bursts of insertions of different retrotransposon families were observed across eukaryotic lineages including Homo sapiens, Zea mays, Oryza sativa, and Blumeria graminis (Shen et al., 1991; SanMiguel et al., 1998; Eichler and Sankoff, 2003; Piegu et al., 2006; Lu et al., 2017; Frantzeskakis et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on TE bursts across species.

claim: In the symbiotic fungus Cenococcum geophilum, the burst of TEs resulted in a dramatically expanded genome compared to closely related species.
source: In the symbiotic fungus Cenococcum geophilum, the burst of TEs resulted in a dramatically expanded genome compared to closely related species (Peter et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on genome expansion in C. geophilum.

claim: A burst of a TE family in brown hydras led to an approximately threefold increase of the genome size compared to related hydras.
source: Similarly, a burst of a TE family in brown hydras led to an approximately threefold increase of the genome size compared to related hydras (Wong et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on genome expansion in hydras.

claim: Across the tree of life, genome sizes vary by orders of magnitude and enlarged genomes invariably show hallmarks of historic TE invasions.
source: Across the tree of life, genome sizes vary by orders of magnitude and enlarged genomes invariably show hallmarks of historic TE invasions (Kidwell, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on genome size variation and TEs.

claim: Population size variation is among the few correlates of genome size across major groups, suggesting that the efficacy of selection plays an important role in controlling TE activity.
source: Population size variation is among the few correlates of genome size across major groups, suggesting that the efficacy of selection plays an important role in controlling TE activity (Lynch, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature and interpreted as evidence for selection's role.

claim: In fungi, TE-rich genomes often show an isochore structure alternating gene-rich and TE-rich compartments.
source: In fungi, TE-rich genomes often show an isochore structure alternating gene-rich and TE-rich compartments (Rouxel et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on fungal genome structure.

claim: TE-rich compartments often harbor rapidly evolving genes such as effector genes in pathogens or resistance genes in plants.
source: TE-rich compartments often harbor rapidly evolving genes such as effector genes in pathogens or resistance genes in plants (Raffaele and Kamoun, 2012; Jiao and Schneeberger, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on gene-TE associations.

claim: Zymoseptoria tritici is one of the most important pathogens on crops, causing high yield losses in many years.
source: The fungal wheat pathogen, Zymoseptoria tritici, is one of the most important pathogens on crops, causing high yield losses in many years (Torriani et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on the pathogen's agricultural impact.

claim: Z. tritici emerged during the domestication of wheat in the Fertile Crescent where the species retained high levels of genetic variation.
source: Z. tritici emerged during the domestication of wheat in the Fertile Crescent where the species retained high levels of genetic variation (Zhan et al., 2005; Stukenbrock et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on the pathogen's evolutionary history.

claim: The pathogen migrated to all temperate zones where wheat is currently grown and underwent multiple migration bottlenecks, in particular when colonizing Oceania and North America.
source: The pathogen migrated to all temperate zones where wheat is currently grown and underwent multiple migration bottlenecks, in particular when colonizing Oceania and North America (Zhan et al., 2005; Estep et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on the pathogen's migration history.

claim: The TE content of the Z. tritici genome shows a striking variation of 17–24% variation among individuals.
source: The TE content of the genome shows a striking variation of 17–24% variation among individuals (Badet et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on TE content variation.

claim: Z. tritici recently gained major TE-mediated adaptations to colonize host plants and tolerate environmental stress.
source: Z. tritici recently gained major TE-mediated adaptations to colonize host plants and tolerate environmental stress (Omrane et al., 2015; Omrane et al., 2017; Krishnan et al., 2018; Meile et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple cited studies on TE-mediated adaptation.

claim: Clusters of TEs are often associated with genes encoding important pathogenicity functions (i.e. effectors), recent gene gains or losses.
source: Clusters of TEs are often associated with genes encoding important pathogenicity functions (i.e. effectors), recent gene gains or losses (Hartmann and Croll, 2017), and major chromosomal rearrangements (Croll et al., 2013; Plissonneau et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on TE-gene associations.

claim: Transposition activity of TEs had a genome-wide impact on gene expression profiles during infection.
source: Transposition activity of TEs also had a genome-wide impact on gene expression profiles during infection (Fouché et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on TE effects on gene expression.

claim: Among primates, genome size varies by ~70% with ~10% between humans and chimpanzees.
source: Among primates, genome size varies by ~70% with ~10% between humans and chimpanzees (Rogers and Gibbs, 2014; Miga et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on primate genome size variation.

claim: In fungi, genome size varies by several orders of magnitude within phyla but is often highly similar among closely related species.
source: In fungi, genome size varies by several orders of magnitude within phyla but is often highly similar among closely related species (Raffaele and Kamoun, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on fungal genome size variation.

claim: Drastic changes in genome size have been observed in the Blumeria and Pseudocercospora genera where genome size changed by 35–130% between the closest known species.
source: Interestingly, drastic changes in genome size have been observed in the Blumeria and Pseudocercospora genera where genome size changed by 35–130% between the closest known species (González-Sayer et al., 2021; Frantzeskakis et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on genome size changes in fungal genera.

claim: In Arabidopsis thaliana genomes, the 45 S rDNA has been shown to have the strongest impact on genome size variation, followed by 5 S rDNA variation, and contributions by centromeric repeats and TEs.
source: In Arabidopsis thaliana genomes, the 45 S rDNA has been shown to have the strongest impact on genome size variation, followed by 5 S rDNA variation, and contributions by centromeric repeats and TEs (Long et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on genome size variation in A. thaliana.

claim: Similar effects of selection on active TEs were observed across plants and animals, including Drosophila melanogaster and Brachypodium distachyon.
source: Similar effects of selection on active TEs were observed across plants and animals, including Drosophila melanogaster and Brachypodium distachyon (Cridland et al., 2013; Stritt et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on selection against TEs in other species.

claim: RTA1-like proteins can function as transporters with a transmembrane domain and have been associated with resistance against several antifungal compounds.
source: One TE insertion is 3815 bp downstream of a gene encoding an RTA1-like protein, which can function as transporters with a transmembrane domain and have been associated with resistance against several antifungal compounds (Soustre et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on RTA1 protein function.

claim: RTA1 proteins show strong copy number variation in several fungi.
source: The nearest gene encodes a RTA1-like protein, a transmembrane exporter that is associated with resistance toward different stressors, including antifungal compounds, and shows strong copy number variation in several fungi (Soustre et al., 1996; Rogers and Barker, 2003; Sirisattha et al., 2004; Ali et al., 2013; Yew et al., 2016; Liang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple cited studies on RTA1 copy number variation.

claim: SNARE domains play a role in vesicular transport and membrane fusion.
source: SNARE domains play a role in vesicular transport and membrane fusion (Bonifacino and Glick, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on SNARE domain function.

claim: Some TE superfamilies have preferred insertion sites in coding regions and transcription start sites.
source: Some TE superfamilies have preferred insertion sites in coding regions and transcription start sites (Miyao et al., 2003; Fu et al., 2013; Gilly et al., 2014; Quadrana et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on TE insertion preferences.

claim: The North American 2015 population experienced the first systematic fungicide applications and subsequent emergence of fungicide resistance in the decade prior to the last sampling.
source: This locus showed a frequency increase only in the more recent North American population, which experienced the first systematic fungicide applications and subsequent emergence of fungicide resistance in the decade prior to the last sampling (Estep et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on fungicide use history.

claim: The TE insertion may have positively modulated RTA1 expression to resist antifungals.
source: Hence, the TE insertion may have positively modulated RTA1 expression to resist antifungals.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the observed association between TE presence and resistance.

claim: Transposition activity in a genome and counteracting purifying selection are expected to establish an equilibrium over evolutionary time.
source: Transposition activity in a genome and counteracting purifying selection are expected to establish an equilibrium over evolutionary time (Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on TE-selection equilibrium.

claim: Temporal bursts of TE families and changes in population size due to bottlenecks or founder events are likely to shift the equilibrium.
source: However, temporal bursts of TE families and changes in population size due to bottlenecks or founder events are likely to shift the equilibrium.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from population genetic theory.

claim: The shallow genome-wide differentiation of Z. tritici populations provides a powerful background to test for outlier loci.
source: The shallow genome-wide differentiation of Z. tritici populations provides a powerful background to test for outlier loci (Hartmann et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on population structure.

claim: The availability of adaptive TE insertions may be a by-product of TE bursts in individual populations.
source: We found the same TE families to have experienced genome-wide copy number expansions, suggesting that the availability of adaptive TE insertions may be a by-product of TE bursts in individual populations.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed correlation between TE bursts and adaptive insertions.

claim: The increase in TEs matches the global colonization history of the pathogen with an increase in TE copies in more recently established populations.
source: The increase in TEs matches the global colonization history of the pathogen with an increase in TE copies in more recently established populations (Zhan et al., 2003; Stukenbrock et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by TE count data and cited literature on colonization history.

claim: Compared to the Israeli population located nearest the center of origin in the Middle East, the European populations showed a threefold increase in TE counts.
source: Compared to the Israeli population located nearest the center of origin in the Middle East, the European populations showed a threefold increase in TE counts.
evidence: The claim is supported by TE count comparisons between populations.

claim: The Australian and North American populations established from European descendants retained high TE counts.
source: The Australian and North American populations established from European descendants retained high TE counts.
evidence: The claim is supported by TE count data and inferred from demographic history.

claim: TE counts nearly doubled over a 25 year period at the North American site.
source: We identified a second increase at the North American site where TE counts nearly doubled again over a 25 year period.
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal comparison of TE counts.

claim: The second expansion at the North American site was driven by a small subset of TE families alone.
source: Compared to the broader increase in TEs from the Middle East, the second expansion at the North American site was driven by a small subset of TE families alone.
evidence: The claim is supported by family-specific TE analysis.

claim: The first expansion in Europe led to an increase in low-frequency variants, suggesting higher transposition activity of many TEs in conjunction with strong purifying selection.
source: Consistent with the contributions from individual TEs, we found that the first expansion in Europe led to an increase in low-frequency variants, suggesting higher transposition activity of many TEs in conjunction with strong purifying selection.
evidence: The claim is supported by frequency spectrum analysis and interpreted through population genetic theory.

claim: The second expansion at the North American site shifted TE frequencies upwards, suggesting relaxed selection against TEs.
source: The second expansion at the North American site shifted TE frequencies upwards, suggesting relaxed selection against TEs.
evidence: The claim is supported by frequency spectrum analysis and interpreted as evidence of relaxed selection.

claim: The population-level context of TEs in Z. tritici shows how heterogeneity in TE control interacts with demography to determine extant levels of TE content and, ultimately, genome size.
source: The population-level context of TEs in Z. tritici shows how heterogeneity in TE control interacts with demography to determine extant levels of TE content and, ultimately, genome size.
evidence: The claim is a synthesis of the study's findings.

claim: Genome size expansions were at least partly caused by the very recent proliferation of TEs.
source: The number of detected TEs was closely correlated with core genome size; hence, genome size expansions were at least partly caused by the very recent proliferation of TEs.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis between TE counts and genome size.

claim: Focusing on the less repetitive core chromosomes in the genome of Z. tritici reduces assembly artifacts substantially.
source: Focusing on the less repetitive core chromosomes in the genome of Z. tritici reduces such artifacts substantially.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of genome assembly challenges and the methodological approach.

claim: Because genome assemblies are the least complete in the most repetitive regions, any under-represented sequences may rather underestimate than overestimate within-species variation in genome size.
source: Because genome assemblies are the least complete in the most repetitive regions, any under-represented sequences may rather underestimate than overestimate within-species variation in genome size.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about assembly biases.

claim: The core genome size differences observed across the species range match genome size variation typically observed among closely related species.
source: The core genome size differences observed across the species range match genome size variation typically observed among closely related species.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to known patterns of genome size variation.

claim: TEs might contribute to genome expansion directly by adding length through additional copies and by increasing the rate of chromosomal rearrangements and ectopic recombination.
source: TEs might not only contribute to genome expansion directly by adding length through additional copies, but also by increasing the rate of chromosomal rearrangements and ectopic recombination (Bourque et al., 2018; Blommaert, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited literature on TE effects on genome structure.

claim: TEs are not the only repetitive elements that can lead to a genome size expansion.
source: However, TEs are not the only repetitive elements that can lead to a genome size expansion.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of other repetitive elements.

claim: Repetitive sequences are drivers of genome size evolution over short evolutionary timescales.
source: In conjunction, recent work demonstrates how repetitive sequences are drivers of genome size evolution over short evolutionary timescales.
evidence: The claim is a synthesis based on the study's findings and broader literature.

claim: Actively transposing elements may accelerate genome evolution and underpin expansions.
source: Actively transposing elements may accelerate genome evolution and underpin expansions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from TE activity patterns.

claim: Genomic defenses should evolve to efficiently target recently active TEs.
source: Hence, genomic defenses should evolve to efficiently target recently active TEs.
evidence: The claim is based on evolutionary reasoning about host-TE dynamics.

claim: TE activity and counteracting genomic defenses have established a tenuous equilibrium across the species range.
source: Here, we show that TE activity and counteracting genomic defenses have established a tenuous equilibrium across the species range.
evidence: The claim is a synthesis of the study's findings.

claim: Population subdivisions are at the origin of highly differentiated TE content within a species matching genome size changes emerging over the span of only decades and centuries.
source: We show that population subdivisions are at the origin of highly differentiated TE content within a species matching genome size changes emerging over the span of only decades and centuries.
evidence: The claim is a synthesis of the study's findings on population-level TE dynamics.

claim: Population-level analyses of genome size can recapitulate genome expansions typically observed across much deeper time scales.
source: In conclusion, population-level analyses of genome size can recapitulate genome expansions typically observed across much deeper time scales providing fundamentally new insights into genome evolution.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the study's approach and findings.

claim: Both the activation of specific TEs and relaxed purifying selection underpin the incipient expansion of the genome.
source: We show that both the activation of specific TEs and relaxed purifying selection underpin this incipient expansion of the genome.
evidence: The claim is a synthesis of the study's findings on mechanisms of genome expansion.

claim: The demographic history likely played a major role in shaping genome evolution within the species.
source: Hence, the demographic history likely played a major role in shaping genome evolution within the species.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the correlation between demographic history and TE/genome size patterns.

claim: Both genome-wide counts of TE insertions and genome size have increased with colonization bottlenecks.
source: We find that both genome-wide counts of TE insertions and genome size have increased with colonization bottlenecks.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TE counts and genome sizes in populations with known bottleneck histories.

claim: Specific TE families have undergone a substantial genome-wide expansion from the pathogen's center of origin to more recently founded populations.
source: We found that specific TE families have undergone a substantial genome-wide expansion from the pathogen's center of origin to more recently founded populations.
evidence: The claim is supported by family-specific TE analysis across populations.

claim: The most dramatic increase in TE insertions occurred between a pair of North American populations collected in the same field at an interval of 25 years.
source: The most dramatic increase in TE insertions occurred between a pair of North American populations collected in the same field at an interval of 25 years.
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal comparison of TE counts at the same location.

claim: Purifying selection substantially depressed TE frequencies in most populations.
source: We show that purifying selection substantially depressed TE frequencies in most populations, but some rare TEs have recently risen in frequency and likely confer benefits.
evidence: The claim is supported by frequency distribution analysis interpreted as evidence of selection.

claim: Some rare TEs have recently risen in frequency and likely confer benefits.
source: We show that purifying selection substantially depressed TE frequencies in most populations, but some rare TEs have recently risen in frequency and likely confer benefits.
evidence: The claim is supported by frequency change analysis and association with beneficial traits.
